lesson.title: One Cell Becomes Two: Mapping the Cell Cycle
lesson.summary: The cell cycle is the ordered sequence of growth, DNA replication, and division that a eukaryotic cell goes through to produce two identical daughter cells, and it relies heavily on the cytoskeleton to carry out that division precisely.
lesson.body:
Every cell in your body arose from an existing cell dividing in two, and every one of those divisions followed the same basic script: the cell cycle. In eukaryotic cells, cells with a true nucleus and organized chromosomes, the cell cycle is the ordered sequence of events a cell goes through between one division and the next. It is traditionally split into two major parts: interphase, made up of the G1, S, and G2 phases, and the mitotic phase, which includes mitosis itself and cytokinesis, the physical division of the cytoplasm into two cells. Interphase takes up the large majority of the cell cycle's time, which surprises people who assume "interphase" means the cell is resting. It is not. A cell in interphase is growing, building proteins and organelles, and, during S phase, copying its entire genome.

The whole point of the cell cycle is to produce two daughter cells that are genetically identical to the parent cell and to each other. That requires the genome to be copied exactly once, with no missed or repeated sections, and then divided so that each daughter cell receives one complete, accurate copy. Given how much can go wrong when copying billions of base pairs and then physically pulling apart chromosomes, the cell cycle includes checkpoints, points at which the cell pauses and verifies that the previous step was completed correctly before committing to the next one. There is a checkpoint near the end of G1 that assesses whether conditions favor division at all, a checkpoint at the end of G2 that verifies DNA replication finished without damage, and a checkpoint during mitosis that confirms chromosomes are properly attached to the machinery that will pull them apart. Each of these gets its own closer look in the phases that follow.

Much of the physical work of the cell cycle depends on the cytoskeleton, the internal scaffolding of protein filaments that gives a cell its shape and lets it reorganize its internal structure. Microtubules, one of the main cytoskeletal filament types, are repurposed during mitosis to build the mitotic spindle, the structure that physically grabs the duplicated chromosomes and pulls them to opposite ends of the cell. Microfilaments, built from the protein actin, take over during cytokinesis, forming a contractile ring that pinches the cell in two once the chromosomes have been separated. The cytoskeleton, in other words, is not a fixed skeleton the cell has at all times, it dismantles and rebuilds itself for different jobs at different points in the cycle.

Not every cell keeps cycling at the same pace, or at all. Cells in tissues that need constant replacement, like the lining of the gut or the outer layers of skin, cycle frequently. Others, like most mature neurons and muscle cells, exit the cycle into a state called G0, a genuinely quiescent phase in which the cell is metabolically active but not preparing to divide, sometimes permanently. Whether a cell stays in G0 or reenters the cycle is largely decided during G1, which is where a closer look at the cycle picks up next.
